contentChunks.htmlValue: Usage

Switches are best used to adjust settings and other standalone options. 

They make a binary selection:

  • On and off

  • True and false

The effects of a switch should start immediately, without needing to save.

contentChunks.footer: Use a switch to turn an option on and off
contentChunks.altText: Toggling a switch turns on dark mode in Settings on a mobile device.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Use switches to:

  • Toggle a single item on or off
  • Immediately activate or deactivate something

contentChunks.footer: Switches are commonly used on mobile to turn settings on or off
contentChunks.altText: Switch used in notification settings to turn on and off the "play over notifications" function.

contentChunks.htmlValue: Switches should be used instead of radio buttons if each item in a set can be independently controlled.

contentChunks.footer: Use radio buttons to toggle items on or off. Radio buttons convey that a set of items are options and can only be selected one at a time. Instead use switches.
contentChunks.altText: Radio buttons used to select Wi-Fi or Bluetooth in the Settings app on a mobile device.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Switches control binary options, not opposing ones. A binary option represents a single selection that's either on or off.

Opposing options are when only one option in a set can be selected at a time, like a list or map view. Use a connected button group instead.

contentChunks.footer: Use a connected button group to choose between opposing options
contentChunks.altText: A connected button group with options of List View and Map View.

contentChunks.footer: Avoid using switches to toggle between opposing options
contentChunks.altText: A switch with non-binary options of List View and Map View.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Alternate selection controls

Checkboxes, radio buttons, and switches are the three main kinds of selection controls. They help people make choices, like selecting options or turning settings on and off.

Use checkboxes to select multiple related options in a list.

Use radio buttons to select a single option in a list.

Use switches to select standalone or more verbose options in a list, like settings.

contentChunks.footer: Checkboxes
contentChunks.altText: 2 checkboxes, 1 unchecked and 1 checked.

contentChunks.footer: Radio buttons
contentChunks.altText: 2 radio buttons, 1 in an enabled state, 1 in a disabled state.

contentChunks.footer: Use checkboxes (not switches) to let people select one or more options from a list
contentChunks.altText: Mobile screen with checkboxes to select list items and call to action button to update the list.

contentChunks.footer: A switch can't replace a button. People expect a call to action to be a button, not a switch.
contentChunks.altText: Mobile screen with checkboxes to select list items and call to action switch to update the list.

contentChunks.footer: Use radio buttons (not switches) when only one item can be selected from a list
contentChunks.altText: Radio buttons used to select a language for a mobile app.

contentChunks.footer: Avoid using a switch to select multiple options that require people to save. Switches should be immediate. Use checkboxes instead.
contentChunks.altText: Mobile screen with switches to select list items and call to action button to update the list.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Icon (optional)

The switch handle can contain an optional icon.

contentChunks.footer: The icon within the handle should always communicate the switch's selection
contentChunks.altText: A checkmark appears on the filled circle of a handle when the switch is toggled on.

contentChunks.htmlValue: Icons can be used to visually emphasize the switch’s selection. The icon’s meaning should be clear and unambiguous to help the people understand whether switch is on or off.

contentChunks.footer: Use icons that clearly communicate whether the switch is on or off, such as an X and a checkmark
contentChunks.altText: 2 switches, the unselected state icon is an X, and the selected state is a checkmark.

contentChunks.footer: Avoid using more ambiguous or non-binary icons, such as a moon or edit icon
contentChunks.altText: A switch’s unselected handle icon is a moon and the selected state icon is a pencil.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Label text

Switches should always be paired with an inline label describing what the switch controls when selected.

contentChunks.footer: Keep labels short and direct. A label should describe what the control does when the switch is on.
contentChunks.altText: Switch label text: 1. Permission manager, App has access to your data. 2. Camera access, app has access to your camera. 3. Show password.

contentChunks.footer: Don't add label text into the switch; the font size would be too small to be accessible. Use an appropriate icon instead.
contentChunks.altText: On a mobile screen’s privacy settings, 2 switches have “On” label text and checkmark icons. The last switch has “Off” label text and no icon.

contentChunks.htmlValue: Placement
Switches are often arranged in stacked layouts.

contentChunks.footer: Settings screens are common places to use switches
contentChunks.altText: Screen showing labels and stacked switches in varying on/off modes.

contentChunks.htmlValue: Behavior
A switch is successfully toggled when the handle slides to the other side of the track after an interaction.

contentChunks.footer: When selected, the switch handle slides to the opposite end of the track
contentChunks.altText: A switch is toggled to turn on airplane mode and Wi-Fi switch automatically turns off.

contentChunks.htmlValue: When a person toggles a switch, its handle size changes and the corresponding action takes effect immediately.

contentChunks.footer: The on state of the switch is indicated by a larger handle size
contentChunks.altText: When selected the switch’s handle gets larger and a checkmark appears on the filled circle.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Use cases

People should be able to do the following with assistive technology:

  • Navigate to a switch with a keyboard or switch input

  • Toggle the switch on and off

  • Get appropriate feedback based on input type documented under Interaction & style
Interaction & style

The switch handle increases in size to indicate interactivity for both touch and cursor control interactions.

Touch
When tapped or dragged, the handle size grows, providing interaction feedback.

Cursor
When hovered (in both on and off states), the hover area grows, providing a visual cue that the handle is interactive. When clicked, the handle size grows.

contentChunks.footer: Touch: Tap, Drag
contentChunks.altText: The switch handle increases in size when tapped and dragged.

contentChunks.footer: Cursor: Hover, Click
contentChunks.altText: The cursor changes from an arrow to a hand pointer when hovering over and clicking the switch.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
Avoid applying density by default

Don't apply density to switches by default — this lowers their targets below our best practice of 48x48 CSS pixels. Instead, give people a way to choose a higher density, like selecting a denser layout or changing the theme.

To ensure that this density setting can easily be reverted when it's active, keep all targets to change it at a minimum 48x48 CSS pixels each.
Initial focus
Initial focus lands directly on the switch’s handle, since it’s the primary interactive element of the component.

contentChunks.footer: Focus lands on the switch handle
contentChunks.altText: The focus is on the switch handle, which is toggled on.

contentChunks.footer: The switch is toggled using Space or Enter
contentChunks.altText: Space or Enter is used to toggle the switch off.

Labeling elements

The accessibility label for a switch uses the adjacent label text if implemented correctly. 

Assistive tech such as a screen reader will read the UI text followed by the component’s role.

contentChunks.footer: A switch’s accessibility label can incorporate its adjacent UI text
contentChunks.altText: “Dark theme” is the switch’s adjacent label text and the accessibility label.

contentChunks.htmlValue:
When the visible UI text is ambiguous, accessibility labels need to be more descriptive. For example, a switch visibly labelled Photo album would benefit from additional information to clarify the switch’s function.

Consider making the adjacent label text more descriptive when possible. This reduces the need for different accessibility text.

contentChunks.footer: While the visible label text reads Photo album, the accessibility label for this switch clarifies its function: Photo album access
contentChunks.altText: The accessibility label for the switch is “Photo album access” though the label text is “photo album.”
